¶
'''Tweed Ring.''' See ''ring''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Tweed’s case.''' See ''case''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tweeg''' (twēg), ''n.'' [Amer. Ind.] The menopome or hellbender, ''Menopoma alleghaniensis.'' See cut under ''hellbender.''

'''tweel''' (twēl), ''n.'' and ''v.'' A Scotch variant of ''twill''<sup>1</sup>. Compare ''tweed.''

'''’tween''' (twēn), ''prep.'' A contraction of ''between.''
{{smaller block|The iron bit he crusheth ’''tween'' his teeth.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 269.}}}}

'''’tween-brain''' (twēn′brān), ''n.'' The cerebral segment between the fore-brain and midbrain; the interbrain; diencephalon, or thalamencephalon. Also ’''twixt-brain.''

'''’tween-deck''' (twēn′dek), ''a.'' Being or lodging between decks.
{{smaller block|The crew and the ’''tween-deck'' passengers.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Jack’s Courtship, xxxviii.}}}}

'''’tween-decks''' (twēn′deks), ''adv.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''between-decks.''
{{smaller block|The blubber is cut into pieces about a foot square and stowed into the ’''tween-decks.'' ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 526.}}

'''tweeny''' (twē′ni), ''n.''; pl. ''tweenies'' (-niz). [< ’''tween'' + ''-y''<sup>2</sup>.] A servant who works between two others, or assists both. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Being in want of a girl to ease both the cook and the housemaid, my wife made her requirements known to some neighbour, who replied, “Oh, yes; I see. You want a ''tweenie.''” ''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VI. 458.}}

¶
'''tweer'''<sup>1</sup>† (twēr), ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''twire''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tweer'''<sup>2</sup> (twēr), ''n.'' [An accom. E. form of F. ''tuyère'': see ''twyer.''] Same as ''twyer.'' ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tweeze, tweese''' (twēz), ''n.'' [See ''twee'', ''étui'', and cf. ''tweezers.''] '''1.''' A surgeons’ case of instruments.
{{smaller block|Drawing a little penknife out of a pair of ''tweezes'' I then chanced to have about me. {{right|''Boyle'', Works, II. 419.}}}}
'''2.''' ''pl.'' Same as ''tweezers'', 1.
{{smaller block|Take anything that ’s given you, purses, knives, handkerchers, rosaries, ''tweezes'', any toy, any money.
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Spanish Gypsy, ii. 1.}}}}

'''tweezer'''<sup>1</sup> (twē′zėr), ''v.'' [< ''tweezer-s'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To use tweezers.
{{smaller block|I like Eichhorn better than Paulus: there is less micrology, less ''tweezering'' at trifles, in his erudition.
{{right|''W. Taylor'', To R. Southey, Dec. 7, 1806 (in Robberd, II. [146).}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To extract with or as with tweezers.
{{smaller block|Having ''tweezered'' out what slender blossom lived on lip or cheek of manhood.
{{right|''Tennyson'', quoted in James Hadley’s Essays, Philol. and [Critical, p. 301.}}}}

'''tweezer'''<sup>2</sup> (twē′zėr), ''n.'' The American merganser. Also called ''weaser.'' ''G. Trumbull'', 1888.

'''tweezer-case''' (twē′zėr-kās), ''n.'' '''1.''' A case for carrying tweezers safely, as about the person, or on a journey.
{{smaller block|<poem>There heroes’ wits are kept in pond’rous vases,
And beaux’ in snuff-boxes and ''tweezer-cases.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., v. 116.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''tweeze'', 1.

'''tweezers''' (twē′zėrs), ''n. pl.'' [Formerly ''tweeser''; prob., with ''-er'' for orig. ''-el'', and by confusion with ''tweeze'', ''tweese'', a var. of E. dial. ''twissel'', a fork of a tree, also a double fruit, < ME. ''twisel'', double (''twisel tunge'', a double tongue), < AS. ''twisel'', fork: see ''twissel''. The word appears to have been confused with ''tweeze'', and in def. 2 is considered a corruption of ''tweezes'', the pl. of ''tweeze'' (cf. ''trousers'' from ''trouses'').] '''1.''' An instrument, resembling diminutive tongs, for grasping and holding: intended for taking up very small objects, plucking out hairs, etc. Also called ''volsella''.
{{smaller block|In the inside of the case were the usual assortment of silk and needles, with scissors, ''tweezers'', &c.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxxviii.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''tweeze'', 1. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tweifold†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''twofold''.

'''tweine†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''twain''.

'''twelfth''' (twelfth), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [With ''-th'' for earlier ''-t'', < ME. ''twelfte'', < AS. ''twelfta'' (= OFries. ''twilifta'', ''tolfta'' = D. ''twaalfde'' = MLG. ''twelfte'', ''twolfte'', LG. ''twolfte'', ''twölfte'' = OHG. ''zwelifto'', ''zwelifte'', MHG. ''zwelfte'', G. ''zwölfte'' = Icel. ''tōlfti'' = Sw. ''tolfte'' = Dan. ''tolvte'' = Goth. *''twalifta''), twelfth; as ''twelve'' + ''-th''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Next in order after the eleventh: an ordinal numeral.—'''2.''' Being one of twelve equal parts into which a whole is regarded as divided.—'''Twelfth cranial nerve''', {{smaller|the hypoglossal, or motor nerve of the muscles of the tongue: in the old enumeration the ''ninth''.}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|twat|6549|Twelfth-day}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|[Found by Browning in the old royalist rimes “Vanity of Vanities,” and, on the supposition that the word denoted “a distinctive part of a nun’s attire that might fitly pair off with the cowl appropriated to a monk,” so used by him in his “Pippa Passes.”]}}

'''twatterlight†''', ''n.'' Same as ''twitterlight.''
{{smaller block|<poem>What mak’st thou here this ''twatterlight?''
I think thou ’rt in a dream.</poem>
{{right|''Wily Beguiled'' (Hawkins, Eng. Dr., III. 331).}}}}

'''twattle''' (twot′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twattled'', ppr. ''twattling.'' [Freq. of *''twat'', < Icel. ''thwætta'', talk, gabble, = Norw. ''twætta'' = Dan. ''tvætte'', jabber, talk nonsense; perhaps connected with Icel. ''thwætti'' in ''ūrthwætti'', slops from wash, refuse (Sw. ''trätta'' = Dan. ''tvætte'', wash), < ''thwā'' = Sw. ''två'' = Dan. ''toe'', wash: see ''towel''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To chatter unmeaningly or foolishly; jabber; gabble; tattle; twaddle.
{{smaller block|Prattlers, which would go from house to house, ''twattling'', and babbling out frothy speech that was good for nothing.
{{right|''W. Whateley'', Redemption of Time (1634), p. 15. (''Latham.'')}}
Idle persons, that will spend whole hours together in ''twattling'' and talking idly, and of other men’s matters.
{{right|''Baxter'', Self-Denial, xxvii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To utter incoherently or foolishly; repeat idly; tattle.
{{smaller block|As readye forgde fittons as true tales vaynelye toe ''twattle.''
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iv. (ed. Arber, p. 101).}}}}

'''2.''' To make much of; fondle; pat, as a horse, cow, dog, etc. ''Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twattle''' (twot′l), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''twattle'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Chatter; gabble; tattle; twaddle. Compare ''twittle-twattle.''—'''2.''' A diminutive person; a dwarf. ''Halliwell.''

'''II.†''' ''a.'' Twattling; trifling; petty.

{{smaller block|They show him the short and ''twattle'' [petits] verses that were written. ''Urquhart,'' tr. of Rabelais, iii. 18. (''Davies.'')}}

'''twattlebasket†''' (twot′l-bȧs″ket), ''n.'' An idle chatterer; a babbler; a prater; a twaddler. ''Bailey,'' 1727.

'''twattler''' (twot′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''twattle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who twattles or prates; a gabbler; a twaddler.

{{smaller block|Let vs, in Gods name, leaue lieng for varlets, berding for ruffians, facing for crakers, chatting for ''twatlers.''
{{right|''Stanihurst,'' Descrip. of Ireland, vi. (Holinshed’s Chron., I.).}}}}

'''twattling''' (twot′ling), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twattle.''] A chatter; a gabbling.

<poem>You keep such a ''twattling'' with you and your bottling;
But I see the sum total, we shall ne’er have a bottle.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Swift,'' To Dr. Sheridan, Dec. 14, 1719.}}}}

'''twattling''' (twot′ling), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Gabbling; prating; twaddling.

{{smaller block|It is not for every ''twattling'' gossip to undertake.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}

'''2.''' Small; trifling; insignificant.

<poem>You feed us with ''twatling'' dishes soe small;
Zounds, a blacke-pudding is better than all.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''King and Miller of Mansfield'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 43).}}}}

'''tway†''' (twā), ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''two.''

'''twayblade''' (twā′blād), ''n.'' [Var. of ''twiblade.''] Primarily, a European orchid, ''Listera ovata'', {{img float|file=century v08 p0353 c1f1.png|width=176px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Twayblade (''Liparis liliifolia''). ''a'', flower.}}}} a simple-stemmed plant a foot or more high, bearing a slender raceme of green flowers, and about six inches from the ground a single pair of broadly ovate leaves, to which the name refers. {{smaller|The name is extended to the other species of the genus, 3 of which are found in North America, ''L. convallarioides'' being the most notable. In America the name is also applied to the members of the genus ''Liparis'', which bear two leaves, springing, however, from the root. ''L. liliifolia'', with purple flowers, is a very handsome species.}}
{{smaller block|In autumn, under the beeches which clothe the long slope of the Quantocks up from Bishop’s Lydiard, you will hardly find any thing, except perhaps a ''tway-blade'' or a herb-paris.
{{right|''The Academy'', April 6, 1889, p. 241.}}}}

'''tweag†, tweague†''' (twēg), ''v. t.'' Old forms of ''tweak''<sup>1</sup>, ''tweak''<sup>2</sup>.

'''tweak'''<sup>1</sup> (twēk), ''v. t.'' [Formerly also ''tweag'', ''tweague''; a var. of ''twick'', unassibilated form of ''twitch''.] '''1.''' To twitch; pinch and pull with or as with a sharp jerk; twinge.
{{smaller block|Now ''tweak'' him by the nose—hard, harder yet.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|Her bones were wrung by rheumatic twinges; her old toes ''tweaked'' with corns.
{{right|''L. Wingfield'', The Lovely Wang, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To put into a fret, perplexity, or dilemma. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''tweak<sup>1</sup>''' (twēk), ''n.'' [< ''tweak''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' A sharp pinch or jerk; a twitch.
{{smaller block|Bobs o’ the Lips, ''Tweaks'' by the Nose, Cuffs o’ the Ear, and Trenchers at my Head in abundance.
{{right|''Brome'', Northern Lass, ii. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' A pinch; dilemma; perplexity: as, to be in a sad ''tweak''. ''E. Phillips'', 1706. Also ''tweag'', ''tweague''.
{{smaller block|I fancy this put the old fellow in a rare ''tweague''.
{{right|''Arbuthnot'', Hist. John Bull, iii. 6.}}}}

'''tweak<sup>2</sup>†''' (twēk), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] '''1.''' A prostitute.
{{smaller block|Your ''tweaks'' are like your mermaids, they have sweet voices to entice the passengers.
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Fair Quarrel, iv. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' A whoremonger. ''Halliwell.''

'''tweasome''' (twē′som), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''twosome''. ''Halliwell.''

'''tweat†''', ''n.'' See ''twaite''<sup>2</sup>.

'''twee''' (twē), ''n.'' [By aphesis from ''etwee'', ''ettwee'', ''étui'': see ''étui''. Cf. ''tweeze''.] Same as ''étui''. ''Planché'', p. 183.

'''tweed''' (twēd), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Said to be an accidental perversion of ''tweel'' for ''twill''<sup>1</sup>: see the quotation.] '''I.''' ''n.'' A twilled fabric, principally for men’s wear, having an unfinished surface, and two colors generally combined in the same yarn. {{smaller|The best quality is made wholly of wool, but in inferior kinds cotton, etc., are introduced. The manufacture is largely carried on in the south of Scotland. The word is sometimes used in the plural.

It was the word “tweels” having been blotted or imperfectly written on an invoice which gave rise to the now familiar name of these goods. The word was read as ''tweeds'' by the late James Locke of London, and it was so appropriate, from the goods being made on the banks of the Tweed, that it was at once adopted, and has been continued ever since. {{right|''Border Advertiser.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}

He was manly, vigorous, and distinguished; nor did he wear at entertainments a shabby suit of mustard-colored ''tweeds.'' {{right|''The Century'', XL. 578.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or made of tweed.
{{smaller block|Round hats and ''tweed'' suits are no sign of independence of thought. {{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XL. 3.}}}}

'''tweedle''' (twē′dl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tweedled'', ppr. ''tweedling.'' [Prob. a var. of ''twiddle'', in sense 3 perhaps by confusion with ''wheedle.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To handle lightly and idly; twiddle; fiddle with.—'''2.''' To play on a fiddle or bagpipe. ''Bailey'', 1731.—'''3†.''' To wheedle; coax.
{{smaller block|A fiddler . . . brought in with him a body of lusty young fellows, whom he had ''tweedled'' into the service. {{right|''Addison'', Freeholder, No. 3.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To wriggle; twist one’s self about.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dick heard, and ''tweedling'', ogling, bridling,
Turning short round, strutting and sideling,
Attested, glad, his approbation.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Pairing Time Anticipated.}}}}

'''tweedle''' (twē′dl), ''n.'' [< ''tweedle'', ''n.''] A sound such as is made by a fiddle.
{{smaller block|[The words ''tweedledum'' and ''tweedledee'' are humorous expansions of ''tweedle'', used together to indicate distinctions that are almost imperceptible.
<poem>Strange all this difference should be
’Twixt ''tweedledum'' and ''tweedledee.''</poem>}}
{{smaller block|{{right|''Byrom'', Feuds between Handel and Buononcini.]}}}}

'''Tweed Ring.''' See ''ring''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Tweed’s case.''' See ''case''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tweeg''' (twēg), ''n.'' [Amer. Ind.] The menopome or hellbender, ''Menopoma alleghaniensis.'' See cut under ''hellbender.''

'''tweel''' (twēl), ''n.'' and ''v.'' A Scotch variant of ''twill''<sup>1</sup>. Compare ''tweed.''

'''’tween''' (twēn), ''prep.'' A contraction of ''between.''
{{smaller block|The iron bit he crusheth ’''tween'' his teeth.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 269.}}}}

'''’tween-brain''' (twēn′brān), ''n.'' The cerebral segment between the fore-brain and midbrain; the interbrain; diencephalon, or thalamencephalon. Also ’''twixt-brain.''

'''’tween-deck''' (twēn′dek), ''a.'' Being or lodging between decks.
{{smaller block|The crew and the ’''tween-deck'' passengers.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Jack’s Courtship, xxxviii.}}}}

'''’tween-decks''' (twēn′deks), ''adv.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''between-decks.''
{{smaller block|The blubber is cut into pieces about a foot square and stowed into the ’''tween-decks.'' ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 526.}}

'''tweeny''' (twē′ni), ''n.''; pl. ''tweenies'' (-niz). [< ’''tween'' + ''-y''<sup>2</sup>.] A servant who works between two others, or assists both. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Being in want of a girl to ease both the cook and the housemaid, my wife made her requirements known to some neighbour, who replied, “Oh, yes; I see. You want a ''tweenie.''” ''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VI. 458.}}

'''tweer'''<sup>1</sup>† (twēr), ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''twire''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tweer'''<sup>2</sup> (twēr), ''n.'' [An accom. E. form of F. ''tuyère'': see ''twyer.''] Same as ''twyer.'' ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tweeze, tweese''' (twēz), ''n.'' [See ''twee'', ''étui'', and cf. ''tweezers.''] '''1.''' A surgeons’ case of instruments.
{{smaller block|Drawing a little penknife out of a pair of ''tweezes'' I then chanced to have about me. {{right|''Boyle'', Works, II. 419.}}}}
'''2.''' ''pl.'' Same as ''tweezers'', 1.
{{smaller block|Take anything that ’s given you, purses, knives, handkerchers, rosaries, ''tweezes'', any toy, any money.
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Spanish Gypsy, ii. 1.}}}}

'''tweezer'''<sup>1</sup> (twē′zėr), ''v.'' [< ''tweezer-s'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To use tweezers.
{{smaller block|I like Eichhorn better than Paulus: there is less micrology, less ''tweezering'' at trifles, in his erudition.
{{right|''W. Taylor'', To R. Southey, Dec. 7, 1806 (in Robberd, II. [146).}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To extract with or as with tweezers.
{{smaller block|Having ''tweezered'' out what slender blossom lived on lip or cheek of manhood.
{{right|''Tennyson'', quoted in James Hadley’s Essays, Philol. and [Critical, p. 301.}}}}

'''tweezer'''<sup>2</sup> (twē′zėr), ''n.'' The American merganser. Also called ''weaser.'' ''G. Trumbull'', 1888.

'''tweezer-case''' (twē′zėr-kās), ''n.'' '''1.''' A case for carrying tweezers safely, as about the person, or on a journey.
{{smaller block|<poem>There heroes’ wits are kept in pond’rous vases,
And beaux’ in snuff-boxes and ''tweezer-cases.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., v. 116.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''tweeze'', 1.

'''tweezers''' (twē′zėrs), ''n. pl.'' [Formerly ''tweeser''; prob., with ''-er'' for orig. ''-el'', and by confusion with ''tweeze'', ''tweese'', a var. of E. dial. ''twissel'', a fork of a tree, also a double fruit, < ME. ''twisel'', double (''twisel tunge'', a double tongue), < AS. ''twisel'', fork: see ''twissel''. The word appears to have been confused with ''tweeze'', and in def. 2 is considered a corruption of ''tweezes'', the pl. of ''tweeze'' (cf. ''trousers'' from ''trouses'').] '''1.''' An instrument, resembling diminutive tongs, for grasping and holding: intended for taking up very small objects, plucking out hairs, etc. Also called ''volsella''.
{{smaller block|In the inside of the case were the usual assortment of silk and needles, with scissors, ''tweezers'', &c.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxxviii.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''tweeze'', 1. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tweifold†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''twofold''.

'''tweine†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''twain''.

'''twelfth''' (twelfth), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [With ''-th'' for earlier ''-t'', < ME. ''twelfte'', < AS. ''twelfta'' (= OFries. ''twilifta'', ''tolfta'' = D. ''twaalfde'' = MLG. ''twelfte'', ''twolfte'', LG. ''twolfte'', ''twölfte'' = OHG. ''zwelifto'', ''zwelifte'', MHG. ''zwelfte'', G. ''zwölfte'' = Icel. ''tōlfti'' = Sw. ''tolfte'' = Dan. ''tolvte'' = Goth. *''twalifta''), twelfth; as ''twelve'' + ''-th''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Next in order after the eleventh: an ordinal numeral.—'''2.''' Being one of twelve equal parts into which a whole is regarded as divided.—'''Twelfth cranial nerve''', {{smaller|the hypoglossal, or motor nerve of the muscles of the tongue: in the old enumeration the ''ninth''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One of twelve equal parts of anything; the quotient of unity divided by twelve. —'''2.''' In ''early Eng. law'', a twelfth of the rents of the year, or of movables, or both, granted or levied by way of tax.—'''3.''' In ''music'', a tone twelve diatonic degrees above or below a given tone, or the interval between two such tones; a compound fifth.—'''4.''' In ''organ-building'', a stop giving tones a twelfth above the normal pitch of the digitals used.—'''5†.''' Twelfth-day. ''Paston Letters'', III. 33.

'''Twelfth-cake''' (twelfth′kāk), ''n.'' A cake prepared for the festivities of Twelfth-night. {{smaller|Into this cake a bean is introduced, and, the cake being divided by lot, whoever draws the piece containing the bean is entitled, as the bean-king, to preside over the ceremonies. In the same way a queen has sometimes been chosen in addition to or instead of a king. Coins have occasionally been substituted for the bean.}}
{{smaller block|Scarcely a shop in London . . . is without ''Twelfth-cakes'' and finery in the windows on Twelfth-day.
{{right|''Hone'', Every-Day Book, I. 50.}}}}
{{smaller block|The celebration of Twelfth-Day with the costly and elegant ''Twelfth-cake'' has much declined within the last half-century.
{{right|''Chambers’s Book of Days'', I. 64.}}}}

'''Twelfth-day''' (twelfth′dā), ''n.'' [< ME. ''Twelthe-day''; < ''twelfth'' + ''day''.] The twelfth day after Christmas; the festival of the Epiphany, occurring on the 6th of January. Also called ''Twelfth-tide''. See ''Epiphany''.
{{smaller block|And my Lord of Wynchestr and my Lord of Seint Jones were with him on the morow after ''Twelthedey'', and he speke to hem as well as ever he did.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 315.}}}}
{{smaller block|In its character as a popular festival, ''Twelfth-Day'' stands only inferior to Christmas. The leading object held in}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
